title: SUBSCRIPTION SALES
content:
A subscription is not simply "something the customer pays for more than once." The reason for the continued payment matters.

In a subscription business, the customer keeps paying because continued payment gives them continued access or value. That could be software they continue using, new content, a community, or ongoing support.

A $600 course paid in six $100 installments is still a one-off purchase if the customer bought the whole course once and is merely paying the balance over time. Likewise, automatically shipping another bottle of a consumable each month does not change the underlying value from replenishment into subscription access.

Subscriptions can create more predictable revenue and higher customer lifetime value, but they also create an ongoing obligation. Customers have to keep deciding that the continuing value is worth the next payment.

CONTINUING PAYMENT REQUIRES CONTINUING VALUE
One customer can generate revenue across multiple billing periods only while the customer believes the next period is worth paying for. Software must remain useful, content must continue to provide value, communities must remain worth belonging to, and ongoing support must keep helping.

CHURN IS PART OF THE MODEL
Customers eventually cancel for many reasons. A subscription therefore cares about how long customers remain and why, not just the first purchase.

THE PAYMENT SCHEDULE IS NOT THE DEFINITION
Collecting installments for a completed purchase is a payment plan. Replacing a used-up product is replenishment. Look for continuing access or value.

CLASSIFICATION EXAMPLES
$600 course paid in six installments -> One-Off with a payment plan.
Monthly box of coffee beans -> Consumable replenishment, even if billed automatically.
$15/month access to software -> Subscription.
$20/month membership with ongoing community access -> Subscription.
Monthly bookkeeping -> Recurring Service, even though billing repeats.

The category follows the value being purchased, not merely the billing frequency.

The central question is:
WHAT CONTINUING VALUE MAKES THE CUSTOMER CHOOSE TO KEEP PAYING?

If that kind of business appeals → PDF 32.
If not → PDF 02.

WHY THE DISTINCTION MATTERS
Calling every repeated charge a subscription can hide the real work of the business. Replenishing coffee requires reliable product supply. Monthly bookkeeping requires repeated labor. Software access requires a product that continues functioning. The payment schedule may look similar while the business underneath it is completely different.

THE CUSTOMER MUST KEEP RECEIVING A REASON TO PAY

A subscription is not defined by that money leaves the customer's account every month. It is defined by continuing value.

Software may keep solving a recurring problem. A content subscription may keep providing new or continually useful material. A membership may provide ongoing access to a community or shared resources. Coaching or support may provide continuing access to help.

That continuing value creates an obligation for the business. If the customer stops seeing a reason to remain, they can cancel. This is why retention and churn matter to subscription models even before you know the technical vocabulary.

PAYMENT PLAN VS SUBSCRIPTION

Suppose a course costs $600 and the customer pays $100 per month for six months. If the customer is simply paying off one completed $600 purchase, the monthly charges do not make the course a subscription.

Now suppose the customer pays $100 each month to remain inside an evolving training library and loses access when they cancel. That is much closer to a subscription because each payment maintains continued access to value.

AUTOSHIP VS SUBSCRIPTION

A monthly shipment of vitamins may also create a monthly charge, but if the customer is paying because last month's vitamins were consumed, the underlying value is replenishment. That belongs in the consumable branch.

RECURRING SERVICE VS SUBSCRIPTION

Monthly bookkeeping can produce recurring revenue too, but the customer is paying for new work to be performed each month. That belongs primarily in the service branch.

These distinctions are not about finding the perfect label. They help you see what the business must keep doing to deserve the next payment.

FOLLOW THE NEXT PAYMENT

Imagine four businesses all charge a customer $30 on the first of each month.

BUSINESS A gives the customer access to software for as long as they keep paying. Cancel the payment and access ends. The next $30 buys another month of access. That is a subscription.

BUSINESS B sends another bag of coffee each month. The next $30 buys another physical unit because the last one was consumed. That is primarily a consumable with automatic replenishment.

BUSINESS C performs bookkeeping work each month. The next $30 buys another period of labor or service. That is a recurring service.

BUSINESS D sold a $180 course and divided the price into six $30 installments. The customer bought one course; the later charges finish paying for that original purchase. That is a payment plan.

The bank statement can look nearly identical. The economic promise is not.

WHY SUBSCRIPTIONS CAN BECOME PREDICTABLE

If customers remain subscribed, a business begins a month with some existing paying relationships instead of starting every sale from zero. That can make revenue more predictable.

But predictability is earned through retention. If 100 customers begin the month and 20 cancel, the business has to replace those 20 just to return to its starting customer count. This loss of subscribers is commonly discussed as churn.

That is why "recurring revenue" is not free money. The model exchanges some pressure to continually create brand-new transactions for a continuing obligation to keep existing customers satisfied enough to remain.

THE QUESTION TO ASK BEFORE CHOOSING SUBSCRIPTION

What will the customer receive in month six that makes month six worth paying for?

If the honest answer is "nothing new; they already got the thing," you may have a one-off product with recurring billing rather than a strong subscription concept.

WHAT CAN CHANGE AS A SUBSCRIPTION GROWS?

Recurring revenue can make growth look deceptively simple. If 100 subscribers are good, 1,000 sounds ten times better.

But ask what else becomes ten times larger.

For software, infrastructure, support requests, security exposure, and maintenance demands may grow.

For content, the same article can serve 1,000 people, so production does not necessarily grow with subscriber count. Customer support and the pressure to maintain a useful publishing system can still grow.

For a community, more members can create more member-to-member value, but also more moderation, administration, conflict, support, and need for structure.

For ongoing coaching or support, growth can run directly into human capacity if each subscriber expects individual attention.

That means subscription is not itself a scalability strategy. The thing being delivered determines how efficiently the subscriber base can grow.

WHAT TO INVESTIGATE BEFORE BUILDING A SPECIFIC SUBSCRIPTION

You do not need a complete retention model yet, but eventually you will need real answers about delivery costs, platform costs, support load, cancellation behavior, payment processing, refunds where applicable, and how much ongoing work the promise requires.

If the subscription depends on a third-party platform, also understand what happens if its price, features, policies, or availability change.

At this stage, the decision is simpler: do you want to build something whose value must remain worth another voluntary payment?

THE DECISION

Choose subscription when continued payment matches continued value you genuinely want to provide. The next question is what the customer keeps receiving or accessing that makes another payment make sense.

You will also see the word CHURN.

Churn means customers canceling or leaving the subscription. If 100 people are subscribed and 10 cancel, those 10 cancellations are churn.

New customers can replace them, but that does not erase the underlying retention question: are existing customers continuing because the subscription remains useful?

WHERE TO GO NEXT
If continued payment for continued value appeals to you, go to PDF 32. If you were mainly attracted to automatic replenishment or repeated client work, consider the Consumable or Service branches instead.
